label: EU(7)-PIM: phenobarbital
title: Phenobarbitone in an older person
statement: Phenobarbital (phenobarbitone) is a medicine to avoid in older people because of the risk of sedation and paradoxical excitation. The 2015 list favoured low doses. Australian Phenobarb tablet information advises against use in severe kidney impairment. Established epilepsy treatment requires prescriber or neurologist review before any dose change because abrupt withdrawal can provoke seizures.

plain_summary: Phenobarbitone is a long-acting sedative and anti-seizure medicine. In people aged 65 and over it can cause heavy sedation or the opposite, agitation.

medicine_groups.name: Phenobarbital
medicine_groups.note: Phenobarbitone is an older name for phenobarbital. Tablets, oral liquids and injections count. Phenobarbital sodium is also called phenobarbitone sodium and counts as the same medicine.

rule_for_models: Suspect a finding when phenobarbitone (phenobarbital) is supplied to a person aged 65 or over. One supply is enough. If age at supply is unknown and the medicine criteria are met, report only a possible finding and ask whether the person was aged 65 or over at supply. An age below 65 rules out this finding.
cannot_be_seen: Supplies alone do not show whether the person takes it for epilepsy, their kidney function or their blood level of phenobarbital. Ask what they take it for and whether they have felt very sleepy or unusually agitated. Epilepsy treatment needs prescriber review before any dose change because stopping suddenly can cause seizures.
ask_the_gp: A review of whether phenobarbitone is still needed. If it treats epilepsy, advice from the neurologist about the plan and any slow change.
